source: Somsak Wannasaree, "Banana Orchards" (Khmer translation, 1997), section 6 (propagation, corm-piece multiplication)
text:
Where a farmer has only a few good mother plants but wants to multiply planting material quickly, a large corm can be cut into pieces to produce more planting units than waiting for natural suckers alone would allow. Each cut piece should carry at least one healthy growth bud, with roughly 5cm of surrounding corm tissue left intact around the bud for protection. From one large corm, this source estimates around 5 usable pieces can typically be cut.

After cutting, the pieces should be dried in the shade for a few days to let the cut surfaces heal over (reducing rot risk) before planting or burying them to sprout; buried at a depth of roughly 15cm, this method can produce on the order of 20 sprouted plantlets from careful handling of the material from a single corm, or scaled up further, on the order of 150 plants from a batch of corm material worked this way.

This method carries more disease risk than simple sucker propagation if the source corm isn't clean, since a wounded cut surface is an easy entry point for soil-borne fungi and bacteria, so it should only be used with corm material known to be free of Fusarium wilt and other soil-borne disease, and cutting tools should be disinfected between corms.
